intro.en: A report collects the readings from the sensors you choose and emails them to the people you choose, on a schedule. This guide makes one from start to finish.

content.text: A report gathers up the readings from the sensors you choose over a period of time, and sends the result to the people you choose, on a schedule. Nobody has to remember to do anything.
A rule tells you the moment something goes wrong. A report tells you how things have been. They answer different questions, and most sites end up using both.
This guide is about making and changing a report. What the finished report contains, and how to read it, is a separate guide.
Have these ready:

items.text: The sensors the report should cover.
How often you want it: daily, weekly, or at the end of each month.
The email address of everybody who should receive it.

content.text: You can save a report and come back to it later. Nothing is sent until the schedule comes round.

content.text: CropWatch calls it a “report template” because it is the recipe, not the finished report. The recipe runs on your schedule and produces a new report each time.

alt.en: The Reports page listing report templates, with the plus button above the list

caption.en: The + button above the list starts a new report.

content.text: The first card is headed “1. Template”.

items.text: — what the people receiving it will see. “Weekly operations summary” is the sort of thing.
— how closely the report looks at the data: every 30 minutes, or every hour. Leave it at 30 minutes unless you have a reason. It does not change how often the report is sent.
— leave it on. Off means the report is kept but never produced, which is how you pause one.

alt.en: Step one of the report form: Name, Description, Data pull interval and the Active template switch

caption.en: The name is what recipients see.

content.text: The second card is headed “2. Device Assignments”. Tick every sensor the report should cover. They are grouped by location, and the box filters as you type.
One report can cover several sensors, and they all appear in the same document. If you would rather each greenhouse had its own report, make one report per greenhouse instead.

alt.en: Step two of the report form, with two sensors ticked under their location

caption.en: Everything you tick ends up in the same report.

content.text: The “Delivery schedule” card decides when a report is produced. There are three switches and a box:

items.text: — one report at the end of each month.
— your time zone, as a number of hours. Japan is 9. Without it, the report is cut off at the wrong time of day and a “daily” report covers the wrong day.

content.text: These are switches, not a choice of one. Turning on both Daily and End of month gives you a report every day and another at the end of the month.
At least one of the three must be switched on. If none is, saving stops and says “Choose at least one cadence (daily, weekly, or monthly) for the active schedule.”

alt.en: The Delivery schedule card with Daily, Weekly and End of month switches, Weekly switched on, and a UTC offset box

caption.en: Weekly, with the UTC offset set to 9 for Japan.

content.text: The “Recipients” card is the list of people who get the report. On a new report there is already one recipient: you, with the email address on your CropWatch account. Change it if somebody else should receive this one.
Press “Add recipient” for each further person, and fill in three things:

items.text: — who it is, so the list makes sense later.

content.text: Add as many as you need. “Remove” takes one off the list, and appears only when there is more than one, so a report always has somebody to go to.

alt.en: The Recipients card with one recipient: Send by Email, an email address and a name, and an Add recipient button

caption.en: Each recipient needs an address and a name.

heading.en: Alerts: the part that is easy to miss

content.text: The “Alerts” card looks optional. It is not. A report with nothing in this card is saved happily and then never produces anything, because the alerts are what tell CropWatch which measurement to put in the report.
Press “Add alert” and fill in:

items.text: — what this one means, such as “Too cold”.
— the number. A Range asks for a “Minimum” and a “Maximum” instead.
— the colour used to mark those readings in the report.

content.text: In the finished report, each alert does three things:

items.text: Readings past the threshold are shaded in its colour, so problems stand out.
A summary line says how many readings matched, and what share of the period that was.
Those readings are always listed, even if the sampling would have skipped over them.

content.text: Alerts here are about temperature, and they never message anybody — they only colour the report. To be told at the time something happens, make an alert rule instead.

alt.en: The Alerts card with one alert: a name, a condition of Less than, a threshold of 5 and a red highlight colour

caption.en: Without at least one of these, the report is never produced.

heading.en: The advanced section, and why to leave it alone

content.text: Below the recipients is a folded-up panel headed “(ADVANCED) Data Processing Schedules”. It throws away readings outside the hours you name — counting only working hours, say.
Its own warning is worth repeating:
“If you do not know what this is, please reach out to support before adding any settings here. Incorrect schedules can silently remove data from your reports.”
Leave it closed. With nothing in it, every reading in the period is used, which is what almost everybody wants.

alt.en: The advanced Data Processing Schedules panel, showing its warning to contact support first

caption.en: Leave this one closed unless support asks you to open it.

content.text: Press “Create Report Template” at the bottom. A green message confirms it and you land back on the list.

If that button is grey and will not press, something is still missing. It stays grey until everything needed is filled in, and a yellow panel headed “Please check these fields” lists what. The usual ones are:

items.text: “Select at least one device for this report template.”
“Choose at least one cadence (daily, weekly, or monthly) for the active schedule.”
A recipient with a missing or misspelled email address.

alt.en: The warning listing what is still missing, with the Cancel and Create Report Template buttons

caption.en: The warning names each thing to fix.

heading.en: Changing, pausing or deleting a report

content.text: Each row on the Reports page has three buttons on the right:

items.text: opens it for changing. The last button then says “Save Changes”.
lists the reports this template has already produced, grouped by sensor, each with a “Download” button. If it says “No reports have been generated yet.”, the first one is still to come.
deletes the template. It asks first: “Are you sure you want to delete the report template …? This cannot be undone.”

content.text: To stop a report for a while, open it and switch “Active template” off rather than deleting it. Reports already sent are not affected by any of this.

alt.en: A row in the reports list with three buttons: a pencil to change it, a clock to see reports already sent, and a bin to delete it

caption.en: The three buttons on each row of the list.

heading.en: Adding notes to a report that has already been sent

content.text: Sometimes a reading needs an explanation: the door was open, the heater was being serviced. You can write that onto a report that has already been produced.

items.text: On the Reports page, press the clock button on the row.
You get the readings for that period. Use the note button on a row to add, change or remove a note, then press “Apply”.
Press “Save Changes” when you have finished.

content.text: The report is rebuilt with your notes on the next scheduled run and kept beside the original. It is not emailed to the recipients again. Notes can be added for up to 23 months after the period ends, and only on air sensors.

items.text: The report saves, and then nothing ever arrives. See
Alerts: the part that is easy to miss
The UTC offset left at zero.
It starts at 0. In Japan it should be 9, or the report is cut off at nine in the morning rather than at midnight.
A report arrives when its schedule comes round, not when you save it.
“Data pull interval” is how closely the data is looked at. The Delivery schedule is how often the report is sent.
Readings can disappear from the report with no warning.
The report still arrives; that sensor is simply missing from it.
